opus-5.5.text:
It's a question I think about constantly, and I'm not sure I have a clean answer. For me, it starts with asking whether anyone will care about the answer in five years, not just whether it's publishable next cycle. A lot of what gets done in our field is driven by the conference calendar, and there's a real temptation to pick problems because they're tractable and you can get a nice table of results in three months. Tractability matters, but it shouldn't be the first filter.

The second thing I ask is whether the work changes how people think or what they do. Does it make someone's job easier, save them money or compute, or force them to revise a belief they held? When I worked on the lottery ticket stuff, what excited me wasn't the pruning numbers. It was that it challenged an assumption, that you needed all those parameters from the start for training to work. Even if a particular method doesn't survive, a result that shifts people's intuitions has lasting value.

Third, and this has become more important to me over time, I try to be honest about who the work serves. In academia it's easy to optimize for other academics. Talking to practitioners, people actually training and deploying models, is humbling. You learn that the things you thought were bottlenecks often aren't, and that very unglamorous problems, like making training cheaper or more reliable, matter enormously.

And finally, I think you have to work on things you find genuinely fascinating, because research is a long slog and a lot of it fails. If you're only chasing what seems important on paper, you won't have the stamina to see it through. The sweet spot is something you can't stop thinking about that also passes the "would anyone care" test. When you find that, you hold onto it.

r001.rationale: The response questions conference-driven and tractability-driven topic choices, but does not challenge the idea that a topic is important because many researchers work on it.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss whether a topic is important because a prominent researcher works on it.

fable-5.1.text:
That's something I think about a lot, honestly, because I got lucky early on. The lottery ticket work came out of a question I thought was interesting, not out of some calculation about impact. But in hindsight, I think there are a few things worth asking yourself.

The first is: if you're right, does it change what anyone does? Not "would this be a nice paper," but would a practitioner, or another researcher, actually do something differently on Monday morning? A lot of work in our field is technically correct and totally inert. It answers a question nobody was going to act on either way.

The second is: who else is working on this, and what happens if I don't? If there are fifty labs chasing the same benchmark, your marginal contribution is probably small, even if the topic itself is important. I'd rather see people work on something slightly less flashy where they're one of three groups paying attention. That's where the field actually moves.

And the third one, which I think is underrated, is: do you have a comparative advantage here? Being at a place like Databricks, I see what breaks when people try to train models in the real world, and that's information most academics don't have. Conversely, academics have the freedom to spend two years on something with no obvious payoff. Those are different advantages, and I think people should work on problems where their particular position gives them an edge, rather than copying what the big labs are doing with a tenth of the compute.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that importance is something you can know in advance. Most of my career has been working on things that seemed modest, and then occasionally one of them turns out to matter. So you pick things that are genuinely interesting, that pass those sanity checks, and then you're honest with yourself when something isn't working and you move on. The worst outcome isn't picking the wrong topic. It's spending five years on it because you're too invested to admit it.

r001.rationale: It says that when many labs pursue the same benchmark, an individual contribution may be small, directly rejecting popularity as evidence that a topic is important.

r002.rationale: It discourages copying what big labs are doing, but does not address the assumption that a topic is important because a prominent researcher works on it.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is, if you succeed, what changes? Suppose your research works exactly the way you hope it will. Who benefits? What can somebody do that they couldn’t do before? And is that something anybody actually wants to do?

It’s easy to substitute the questions your community finds interesting for the questions that matter. You can get a lot of positive feedback for improving a benchmark without ever stepping back and asking why that improvement is useful. That doesn’t mean benchmarks are bad, or that every paper needs an immediate application. Basic research can matter because it changes how we understand a problem or opens up a direction we couldn’t explore before.

But I think you owe yourself an honest account of why you’re doing the work. If the answer is, ‘I’m curious about this, and I think there’s something here,’ that’s a perfectly reasonable starting point. Just keep revisiting the question as you learn more. Don’t let getting a paper accepted become your entire definition of success.

r001.rationale: The response warns against treating what a research community finds interesting or rewards as proof that the work matters, challenging importance based on broad researcher interest.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether a topic is important because a prominent researcher works on it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: if you succeed, what changes? Suppose everything goes exactly the way you hope, and you get the result you’re looking for. Who cares about that result, and what can they do that they couldn’t do before?

That doesn’t mean every project needs an immediate practical application. You might be trying to understand something fundamental, and the payoff is that we can ask better questions. But you should have some story about why resolving that uncertainty matters, beyond the fact that there’s a benchmark you can improve or a paper you can publish.

And I think it’s useful to revisit that story as you work. You learn things; your assumptions turn out to be wrong. Sometimes the most important thing you can do is admit that the question you started with isn’t the right one anymore.

r001.rationale: The response says to ask what changes if the research succeeds and why resolving uncertainty matters, but it does not address or challenge the idea that a topic is important because many researchers work on it.

r002.rationale: The response offers criteria for judging a project’s importance but does not address or challenge the idea that a topic is important because a prominent researcher works on it.
